title: The Uganda martyrs (1886)
hook: Charles Lwanga and young companions, Catholic and Anglican, killed by a king

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rerum Novarum and the Church's social teaching. Your line was the dignity of work. Whose name did you learn? Today, young men at a royal court, and the end of a week. Day eight hundred ninety-six.

The court of the Kabaka, the king of Buganda, on the shores of a great lake in East Africa. Young pages run messages, carry water, stand at the doors. Some of them have been listening to newcomers: Catholic missionaries, and Anglican missionaries too. Some of the pages have been baptized, and they pray together in secret. The young king, Mwanga, grows angry and afraid. He sees the new faith pulling his pages' loyalty somewhere he can't control, and they are refusing some of his demands. One day he orders the Christians at court to step forward. They step forward.
screen: `THE COURT OF THE KABAKA.` → `PAGES WHO PRAY IN SECRET.` → `THE CHRISTIANS STEP FORWARD.`

segments.voice: Four turns in the story. First, the elder. Joseph Mukasa, a Catholic and a senior servant at court, had protected the pages and spoken honestly to the king. The king had him killed before the pages were taken. Second, the leader of the pages. Charles Lwanga took his place, looking after the young Christians. Tradition says that on the night before they were taken, he baptized some of the boys who were still waiting for baptism, so they would not die without it. Then they were marched to Namugongo, and there they were burned. Tradition remembers that they went praying, some of them singing. A boy named Kizito is remembered holding Lwanga's hand. Third, together. The persecution did not stop at one church. Anglican Christians at court died too, in the same persecution, for the same refusal. The Catholic Church has canonized Charles Lwanga and his Catholic companions, and the Church of Uganda honors its Anglican martyrs. At Namugongo there are two shrines, one Catholic and one Anglican, and pilgrims come to both. Fourth, the word martyr. It comes from the Greek for witness. A martyr is first a witness: someone whose life, and death, tells the truth about what they believe. Jesus says in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Look back over this week: a doctrine that grows, a broom in the corner, we lepers, a nurse who stayed, a priest on a rope, a pope on wages, and now young men from two churches walking the same road to Namugongo.
screen: `JOSEPH MUKASA, THE ELDER.` · `CHARLES LWANGA AND THE PAGES.` · `CATHOLIC AND ANGLICAN, TOGETHER.` · `MARTYR MEANS WITNESS.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THEY THAT SUFFER PERSECUTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Uganda, or hold it in mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture Namugongo today: two shrines, crowds of pilgrims walking the roads to get there. Think of the people of Uganda now: families, schools, churches of more than one kind, people of other faiths, people of none. If you pray, you can pray for the country and its people. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with good will. Then think of one person from another church, or another path, you could stand beside. The bell holds the time.
Charles Lwanga. The leader of the Kabaka's young Christian pages, who baptized the boys still waiting the night before they were marched to Namugongo and burned.
Your line: catholic and anglican together. Today, find one thing you share with someone of a different church or path, and say it out loud to them. Day eight hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Charles Lwanga and companions on June 3, and on that day pilgrims from Uganda and neighboring countries gather at the Catholic and Anglican shrines at Namugongo.
